voice.reference_text: 大家好，欢迎来到 AI 高频词。每一期，我们只讲清楚一个词：它解决什么问题，怎么理解它，以及它在现实里意味着什么。

items.text: Your phone can find your cat in your photos, yet nobody ever gave it rules for what a cat looks like.
So how does it do it? It saw tons of examples and worked out the patterns itself. That's today's AI.
A traditional program works differently: people write the rules one by one, and the computer follows them.
For payroll or booking flights, the rules are clear, so that's enough.
But some things are hard to write rules for, like reading a handwritten three. Fat, skinny, tilted, you know it instantly.
Now try writing down how. "Two curves stacked"? So is an eight. "Bottom half opens left"? So does a five.
Rules like that miss some threes and mistake other digits for threes.
So most of today's AI flips it around: no rules, just examples.
Show the computer hundreds or thousands of handwritten digits, each with its answer: this is a three, this is a seven.
It finds the patterns itself, and that's called machine learning.
What it learns is called a model. Show the model a new image, and it gives you an answer.
A lot of people think programmers coded in everything AI can do. Mostly, it learned from examples, which we call data.
Let's actually try it, with nearly eighteen hundred handwritten digits, each a tiny eight-by-eight grid.
First we lock away three hundred as the test, and the rest are examples to learn from.
Learning from them is called training, and during training it never sees a test question.
Only questions it hasn't seen can show whether it truly learned, or just memorized.
So, take a guess: with just ten examples, how much of the test does it get right?
Pick ten at random, and often some digits don't show up at all.
We tried twenty different random sets of ten. The typical score was about thirty-seven percent: better than the ten percent you'd get guessing, but still low.
With a hundred examples, it gets eighty-eight percent. With all fifteen hundred or so, it gets ninety-seven percent.
We never gave it rules for a three, just told it which ones were threes. In this experiment, more examples meant better scores.
Still, it missed ten of the three hundred, like this messy two it called a one.
Here's another way to see it: today's AI is a prediction machine. Not predicting the future, just seeing something and guessing the answer.
Our model also says how sure it is. It's ninety-six percent sure this one's a three.
Other AI works the same way. Give a language model half a sentence, and it guesses the next word, then the next, until there's a whole answer.
Chatbots built on large language models reply this way.
They guess well, but a convincing answer can still be wrong.
So how do all these terms fit together? Picture AI, artificial intelligence, as the biggest circle: computers doing things that seem to take smarts.
A chess program built on hand-written rules counts as AI. A plain payroll program doesn't.
Inside AI is machine learning, and inside that, deep learning, which runs on neural networks: many layers of simple math.
"Deep" just means many layers, not deep understanding. Large language models are built with deep learning.
When I say "today's AI," I mean machine learning: AI that learns from examples.
Learning from data can go wrong, too. According to Reuters, Amazon once tried using AI to screen résumés.
It learned from ten years of résumés sent to the company, mostly by men.
In effect, it taught itself that male candidates were better.
Résumés with the word "women's," as in "women's chess club captain," got marked down.
The tool was later scrapped. If the data is biased, the model can pick that up too.
When you use AI, remember three things.
First, it may answer anyway, even about things it's never seen. Show our digit model the letter A, and it still has to pick from zero to nine.
It says it's ninety-two percent sure that's a four. But it can only pick from the ten digits.
A kid would say, "That's not a number." The model won't.
Second, it gives you predictions, not the truth. Remember that messy two? The model was eighty-one percent sure it was a one, and it was wrong.
Third, what it gets right or wrong depends on its data, and also on how it's designed and trained.
So to judge whether an AI is reliable, first find out what data it learned from.
Whenever an AI sounds totally sure, ask yourself: has it seen questions like this before?
Most of today's AI isn't built on rules people write. It learns patterns from examples.
Next time, we'll look at why a model can ace the practice questions and still stumble on new ones. That's often a sign of overfitting.
